title: Inside the Pokémon World Championships: 50,000 Fans, One Blinking Motorcycle
summary:
What if your favorite video game characters came to life? In August, at the Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco, that's exactly what happened. Kid Reporter Adam Sadi was there, and he shared his experience.

The event, called Worlds for short, drew 50,000 visitors to the Moscone Center. Outside, giant Pokémon lined a decorated road with food stands and giant Lego sets. Music and cheering filled the air as characters paraded through the crowd. Inside, serious battles took place—some on video game consoles, others with trading cards across tables.

For beginners like Adam, Pokémon Professors taught the rules of the Trading Card Game. But kids who had practiced for years competed against the best in the world. Adam met Haruki Okunishi, a top junior player and champion who had traveled from Malaysia. Haruki's strategy? "I just practice and practice!" he said. Some matches last an hour of battling tough opponents, but Haruki reminded Adam that it's still a lot of fun.

Competition was only part of the magic. One fan, dressed as Umbreon, drove seven hours to attend. Another, dressed as Absol, told Adam that Pokémon "brings together people of all backgrounds and all ages." Looking around at kids, teens, parents, competitors, and cosplayers, it was easy to see that.

Downstairs, Adam found two Pokémon unlike any others: the Honda Koraidon and Toyota Miraidon. These are full-size, futuristic, rideable motorcycle Pokémon. As Adam watched, Koraidon blinked at him!

Pokémon is now 30 years old, but at Worlds, it didn't feel old at all. The world behind the cards and screens suddenly felt alive and huge, full of people still imagining it together.
why_it_matters: Worlds shows how a game invented for children in the 1990s can still shape global culture, tourism and even car design, and how shared hobbies — not just school or family — become places where very different people find common ground. It is also big business, with cities and companies competing for the attention of tens of thousands of fans.

background_read: Pokémon began in Japan in the 1990s as a pair of video games for a handheld console, and grew into one of the world's biggest franchises, with trading cards, TV series, films and toys — the article notes it is now 30 years old.

The Pokémon World Championships (nicknamed 'Worlds') is that franchise's biggest annual tournament, run for video game and Trading Card Game players for over two decades, with competitors split into age divisions such as junior and masters.
Cosplay (dressing up as a character) grew out of Japanese fan events in the 1980s and is now a standard part of big conventions, which is why Umbreon and Absol costumes fit right in at Worlds.
Malaysia, where the junior champion Haruki Okunishi travelled from, is a country in Southeast Asia.

The Moscone Center is a large convention hall in San Francisco that also hosts major technology conferences, while Honda and Toyota (two of the world's biggest car makers, both based in Japan) built the full-size rideable 'motorcycle Pokémon' — Koraidon and Miraidon, legendary Pokémon from the games Scarlet and Violet that look like motorbikes.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — fans, beginners and the host city
perspectives.description: Worlds is a shared celebration: 50,000 visitors, cosplayers, families and elite competitors in one hall, plus a boost for hotels, restaurants and shops in San Francisco. Newcomers are welcomed too, taught the card game by Pokémon Professors instead of being left on the sidelines.

Travelling to a championship can be expensive for families, and rare cards and merchandise can turn collecting into a spending race that prices some kids out. A 50,000-person event also leaves a large environmental footprint and can feel unwelcoming to players who cannot keep up.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — how a franchise stays alive for 30 years
perspectives.description: Worlds is a case study in 'transmedia': the same world is experienced through games, cards, films and live events, so each one advertises the others. Long-lived brands survive by giving fans a place to meet in person, not only products to buy.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what the next decade looks like
perspectives.description: As Pokémon passes 30, it faces familiar questions: how to keep growing without exhausting fans, whether to push harder into esports with bigger prizes and broadcasts, and how events like Worlds can be made cheaper, greener and easier to reach for players outside Japan, the US and Europe.
